The folly of trusting Egypt (verses 1–5)

God opposes the help that his people seek from those who practice wickedness.

Sinners can sometimes recognize how foolish their actions are when the truth is stated plainly. Yet they may still refuse to live as though they believed it.

No one can escape God's judgments; evil follows the unrepentant.

The Lord of hosts will come to defend Mount Zion.

The Lion of the tribe of Judah will fight for his church.

He will also protect Jerusalem with the tenderness of birds hovering over their young, sheltering them from harm.

God's protection joins great strength with profound compassion.

His people may trust him to preserve them.

Backsliders called to return (verses 6–9)

Israel had wandered far from God.

Yet they were still described as his children.

Let them turn back, and the Lord will heal their backsliding, however deeply sin has brought them into misery.

People often make idols of silver and gold.

Love of possessions draws hearts away from God.

Those who truly repent become ready to surrender whatever they have treated as a rival to him.

When the people abandoned their idols, the Assyrian would fall through an angel's sword.

That messenger strikes with more power than a mighty warrior, though more quietly and unexpectedly than an ordinary person.

God can make even the bravest human heart tremble.

Meanwhile, if his people keep the fire of holy love and devotion burning in their hearts and homes, they may depend upon his protection.

The sin and folly of seeking help from Egypt. ( [Isa.31.1-Isa.31.5] Is. 31:1-5) God's care for Jerusalem. ( [Isa.31.6-Isa.31.9] Is. 31:6-9)
Verses 1-5 God will oppose the help sought from workers of iniquity. Sinners may be convicted of folly by plain and self-evident truths, which they cannot deny, but will not believe. There is no escaping the judgments of God; and evil pursues sinners. The Lord of hosts will come down to fight for Mount Zion. The Lion of the tribe of Judah will appear for the defence of his church. And as birds hovering over their young ones to protect them, with such compassion and affection will the Lord of hosts defend Jerusalem. He will so defend it, as to secure its safety.
[Isa.31.6-Isa.31.9]
Verses 6-9 They have been backsliding children, yet children; let them return, and their backslidings shall be healed, though they have sunk deep into misery, and cannot easily recover. Many make an idol of their silver and gold, and by the love of that are drawn from God; but those who turn to God, will be ready to part with it. Then, when they have cast away their idols, shall the Assyrian fall by the sword of an angel, who strikes more strongly than a mighty man, yet more secretly than a mean man. God can make the stoutest heart to tremble. But if we keep up the fire of holy love and devotion in our hearts and houses, we may depend upon God to protect us and them.

Christ the righteous King and shelter (verses 1–8)

Jesus Christ is the righteous King promised here, and his faithful disciples share in the benefits of his reign.

The consolation and grace of his Spirit resemble rivers flowing through a dry land.

A traveler crossing a desert finds refreshing shade beneath a great overhanging rock.

Likewise, Christ's power, truth and love provide believers with their only lasting protection and refreshment as they journey toward heaven.

Christ bore the storm himself to keep it from falling upon us.

Let frightened sinners flee to him, for he alone can shelter and renew them in every trial.

Notice how much effort wicked people put into wrongdoing.

They work hard at it, direct their hearts toward it and develop clever plans to accomplish it.

Yet our comfort is that they cannot do more harm than God permits.

Let us pray to be freed from selfishness.

A truly generous soul thinks of generous things concerning God.

Such a person asks him for wisdom and discernment, the comfort of his presence, the influence of his Spirit and, in due time, the full enjoyment of his glory.

Trouble overcome through the outpouring of the Spirit (verses 9–20)

When a people have greatly provoked the holy Lord, difficult times should not surprise them.

Many careless people refuse generosity while using their possessions for self-indulgence.

We deserve to lose earthly provisions when we use them chiefly to nourish sinful desires.

Let those who live in that way be afraid and awaken.

A genuinely blessed age arrives through the outpouring of the Spirit from above.

Only then will lasting good times come.

Henry understands the present condition of the Jewish people as continuing until a fuller outpouring of the Holy Spirit, which he still expects.

Peace and quietness grow from righteousness.

Lasting satisfaction exists only in true religion.

Real holiness is real happiness even now. In heaven, where holiness becomes perfect, happiness will also be perfect forever.

The good seed of God's word will be scattered widely.

Divine grace will water it, and patient, hardworking servants will be sent into the Lord's field.

Times of peace and happiness. ( [Isa.32.1-Isa.32.8] Is. 32:1-8) An interval of trouble, yet comfort and blessings in the end. ( [Isa.32.9-Isa.32.20] Is. 32:9-20)
Verses 1-8 Christ our righteous King, and his true disciples, are evidently here intended. The consolations and graces of his Spirit are as rivers of water in this dry land; and as the overhanging rock affords refreshing shade and shelter to the weary traveller in the desert, so his power, truth, and love, yield the believer the only real protection and refreshment in the weary land through which he journeys to heaven. Christ bore the storm himself, to keep it off from us. To him let the trembling sinner flee for refuge; for he alone can protect and refresh us in every trial. See what pains sinners take in sin; they labour at it, their hearts are intent upon it, and with art they work iniquity; but this is our comfort, that they can do no more mischief than God permits. Let us seek to have our hearts more freed from selfishness. The liberal soul devises liberal things concerning God, and desires that He will grant wisdom and prudence, the comforts of his presence, the influence of his Spirit, and in due time the enjoyment of his glory.
[Isa.32.9-Isa.32.20]
Verses 9-20 When there was so much provocation given to the holy God, bad times might be expected. Alas! how many careless ones there are, who support self-indulgence by shameful niggardliness! We deserve to be deprived of the supports of life, when we make them the food of lusts. Let such tremble and be troubled. Blessed times shall be brought in by the pouring out of the Spirit from on high; then, and not till then, there will be good times. The present state of the Jews shall continue until a more abundant pouring out of the Spirit from on high. Peace and quietness shall be found in the way and work of righteousness. True satisfaction is to be had only in true religion. And real holiness is real happiness now, and shall be perfect happiness, that is, perfect holiness for ever. The good seed of the word shall be sown in all places, and be watered by Divine grace; and laborious, patient labourers shall be sent forth into God's husbandry.

God defeats the proud destroyer (verses 1–14)

The deceitful and proud destroyer will answer for violence and fraud.

The righteous Lord sometimes repays wicked people in the same manner in which they treated others.

Those who wait humbly upon God through faith will find him gracious.

As each day comes, so may the strength for that day come.

If God abandoned us to ourselves for even one morning, we would be lost.

We should therefore place ourselves in his hands every morning, and undertake the day's work through his strength.

When he rises to defend his people, his enemies scatter.

True knowledge and wisdom lead to the strength of salvation, making us steadfast in God's ways.

True devotion is the only treasure that cannot be robbed or consumed.

Jerusalem faced terrible suffering.

But God's time to help his people often comes precisely when every other helper has failed.

Everyone who hears what God has accomplished should recognize that he is able to do all things.

Sinners within Zion must answer for privileges they knowingly abused, an accountability greater than that of others.

Those who reject the commands of God's word cannot claim its comforts when distress arrives.

God's wrath against unrepentant sin is pictured as unquenchable fire: the justice of the eternally living God confronting the guilt of a soul that does not cease to exist.

The security and joy of the upright (verses 15–24)

True believers remain watchful against opportunities to sin.

God's power keeps them safe; faith in that power enables them to remain at peace.

They will not lack anything truly necessary for their ultimate good.

The blessings of salvation are freely given to all who seek God in humble, believing prayer.

The upright receive bread and water, but they also see the King in his beauty—the beauty of holiness.

Remembering earlier terrors deepens the joy of deliverance.

It is good to enjoy peace in one's own home, but better still to enjoy peace in God's house.

Christ will always preserve people who serve him.

Jerusalem had no large river flowing past it.

Yet God's presence and power were sufficient to supply every need.

Through faith we receive Christ as Prince and Savior, reigning over his redeemed people.

Those who refuse his reign place their souls in peril.

Illness is removed mercifully when its spiritual result is that sin is taken away.

If guilt has been pardoned, believers have far less reason to complain about bodily suffering.

The final verse points beyond earthly blessing toward heaven, where sickness and trouble cannot enter.

The One who blots out our transgressions will also heal our souls.

[Isa.33.1-Isa.33.14]
Chapter 33
God's judgments against the enemies of his church. ( [Isa.33.1-Isa.33.14] Is. 33:1-14) The happiness of his people. ( [Isa.33.15-Isa.33.24] Is. 33:15-24)
Verses 1-14 Here we have the proud and false destroyer justly reckoned with for all his fraud and violence. The righteous God often pays sinners in their own coin. Those who by faith humbly wait for God, shall find him gracious to them; as the day, so let the strength be. If God leaves us to ourselves any morning, we are undone; we must every morning commit ourselves to him, and go forth in his strength to do the work of the day. When God arises, his enemies are scattered. True wisdom and knowledge lead to strength of salvation, which renders us stedfast in the ways of God; and true piety is the only treasure which can never be plundered or spent. The distress Jerusalem was brought into, is described. God's time to appear for his people, is, when all other helpers fail. Let all who hear what God has done, acknowledge that he can do every thing. Sinners in Zion will have much to answer for, above other sinners. And those that rebel against the commands of the word, cannot take its comforts in time of need. His wrath will burn those everlastingly who make themselves fuel for it. It is a fire that shall never be quenched, nor ever go out of itself; it is the wrath of an ever-living God preying on the conscience of a never-dying soul.
[Isa.33.15-Isa.33.24]
Verses 15-24 The true believer watches against all occasions of sin. The Divine power will keep him safe, and his faith in that power will keep him easy. He shall want nothing needful for him. Every blessing of salvation is freely bestowed on all that ask with humble, believing prayer; and the believer is safe in time and for ever. Those that walk uprightly shall not only have bread given, and their water sure, but they shall, by faith, see the King of kings in his beauty, the beauty of holiness. The remembrance of the terror they were in, shall add to the pleasure of their deliverance. It is desirable to be quiet in our own houses, but much more so to be quiet in God's house; and in every age Christ will have a seed to serve him. Jerusalem had no large river running by it, but the presence and power of God make up all wants. We have all in God, all we need, or can desire. By faith we take Christ for our Prince and Saviour; he reigns over his redeemed people. All that refuse to have Him to reign over them, make shipwreck of their souls. Sickness is taken away in mercy, when the fruit of it is the taking away of sin. If iniquity be taken away, we have little reason to complain of outward affliction. This last verse leads our thoughts, not only to the most glorious state of the gospel church on earth, but to heaven, where no sickness or trouble can enter. He that blotteth out our transgressions, will heal our souls.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesGod's vengeance against the enemies of his church.1–8Their desolation.9–17
Judgment against the enemies of God's church (verses 1–8)

Isaiah describes the Lord's wars, whose purposes are righteous and whose final outcome is certain.

The warning concerns all nations.

All have benefited from God's patience; those refusing to repent must also reckon with his judgment.

The fearful description of bloodshed should impress upon our minds the seriousness of divine justice.

Henry interprets Idumea as representing the peoples set against God's church, including what he calls the kingdom of Antichrist.

The full terror of the final day awaiting people who persist in opposing Christ is beyond human comprehension.

God has appointed the time when his church will be delivered and its enemies brought down.

Until that day, we should wait patiently and not pronounce final judgments before the appointed time.

Through Jesus Christ, the Lord can show mercy to believers without compromising righteousness.

In this way he glorifies his own name.

The barrenness left by sin (verses 9–17)

Those who try to destroy God's church will never succeed in their ultimate purpose.

Instead they bring ruin upon themselves.

What dreadful changes sin can cause!

It can turn fertile countryside into wasteland and transform a crowded city into an uninhabited wilderness.

Let us compare everything we discover in the book of the Lord with the movements of Providence around us.

Then we will seek his kingdom and righteousness more diligently.

What the Lord commands through his mouth, his Spirit will accomplish.

As the predictions of Scripture are fulfilled, the evidence of its truth continues to grow, leading toward the time when these scenes of judgment give way to better days.

Henry interprets Israel as a figure of Christ's church, and the Edomites—Israel's bitter enemies—as figures of the enemies of Christ's kingdom.

God's Jerusalem may be reduced to ruins for a period.

But the enemies who persist in opposing his church face a desolation that lasts forever.
classic_reading:
[Isa.34.1-Isa.34.8]
Chapter 34
God's vengeance against the enemies of his church. ( [Isa.34.1-Isa.34.8] Is. 34:1-8) Their desolation. ( [Isa.34.9-Isa.34.17] Is. 34:9-17)
Verses 1-8 Here is a prophecy of the wars of the Lord, all which are both righteous and successful. All nations are concerned. And as they have all had the benefit of his patience, so all must expect to feel his resentment. The description of bloodshed suggests tremendous ideas of the Divine judgments. Idumea here denotes the nations at enmity with the church; also the kingdom of antichrist. Our thoughts cannot reach the horrors of that awful season, to those found opposing the church of Christ. There is a time fixed in the Divine counsels for the deliverance of the church, and the destruction of her enemies. We must patiently wait till then, and judge nothing before the time. Through Christ, mercy is exercised to every believer, consistently with justice, and his name is glorified.
[Isa.34.9-Isa.34.17]
Verses 9-17 Those who aim to ruin the church, can never do that, but will ruin themselves. What dismal changes sin can make! It turns a fruitful land into barrenness, a crowded city into a wilderness. Let us compare all we discover in the book of the Lord, with the dealings of providence around us, that we may be more diligent in seeking the kingdom of God and his righteousness. What the mouth of the Lord has commanded, his Spirit will perform. And let us observe how the evidences of the truth continually increase, as one prophecy after another is fulfilled, until these awful scenes bring in more happy days. As Israel was a figure of the Christian church, so the Edomites, their bitter enemies, represent the enemies of the kingdom of Christ. God's Jerusalem may be laid in ruins for a time, but the enemies of the church shall be desolate for ever.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe flourishing state of Christ's kingdom.1–4The privileges of his people.5–10
The wilderness blossoms through grace (verses 1–4)

Judah prospered under Hezekiah, but the main subject of this prophecy, according to Henry, is Christ's kingdom.

Converting grace makes a soul that was once a wasteland rejoice and sing, and grow abundantly like a garden filled with flowers.

The gospel encourages the weak and fearful.

Fear weakens us; resisting fear strengthens us both for the tasks we must do and for the suffering we may have to endure.

The One who calls us to be strong has made help available through One who is mighty.

The Messiah would come to confront the powers of darkness and bring generous consolation to those who mourn in Zion.

He will come and save.

He will also come again at the end of time to judge those who oppressed his people and give the afflicted a rest that fully compensates their suffering.

The highway of holiness and eternal joy (verses 5–10)

When Christ establishes his kingdom, he works great wonders within human souls.

Through his word and Spirit, those spiritually blind begin to see.

Those who were deaf to God's calls become willing listeners.

People unable to do good receive grace to act faithfully.

Those who did not know how to speak about God or to God receive opened lips that praise him.

When the Holy Spirit came upon Gentiles hearing the gospel, the fountains of spiritual life were opened.

Much of the earth still resembles a desert, lacking the means of grace, faithful worshipers and the fruits of holiness.

But the path of godliness will be opened.

The highway of holiness is the way of God's commandments, the good and ancient way.

It is a clear road toward heaven.

Even uneducated people who know little may be kept from missing it.

It is also a safe road, for nothing can ultimately harm those traveling on it.

Jesus Christ is the way to God.

He is clearly revealed, and the duties of faithful people are plainly marked out.

Let us therefore go forward cheerfully, assured that our destination is everlasting joy and rest for the soul.

Those who enter gospel Zion by faith rejoice in Jesus Christ.

Divine consolation causes sorrow and sighing to flee.

Such hopes and expectations of eternity should overshadow both the sorrows and the fleeting delights of this present life.

Yet merely admiring Scripture's beauty is not enough.

Do we personally possess its promises through faith?

Do we love God not only as Creator but because he gave his only Son to die for us?

Are we truly walking in holiness?

These practical questions are far more useful than spending our time on curious, amusing but fruitless speculation.

[Isa.35.1-Isa.35.4]
Chapter 35
The flourishing state of Christ's kingdom. ( [Isa.35.1-Isa.35.4] Is. 35:1-4) The privileges of his people. ( [Isa.35.5-Isa.35.10] Is. 35:5-10)
Verses 1-4 Judea was prosperous in the days of Hezekiah, but the kingdom of Christ is the great subject intended. Converting grace makes the soul that was a wilderness, to rejoice with joy and singing, and to blossom abundantly. The feeble and faint-hearted are encouraged. This is the design of the gospel. Fear is weakening; the more we strive against it, the stronger we are, both for doing and suffering; and he that says to us, Be strong, has laid help for us upon One who is mighty. Assurance is given of the approach of Messiah, to take vengeance on the powers of darkness, to recompense with abundant comforts those that mourn in Zion; He will come and save. He will come again at the end of time, to punish those who have troubled his people; and to give those who were troubled such rest as will be a full reward for all their troubles.
[Isa.35.5-Isa.35.10]
Verses 5-10 When Christ shall come to set up his kingdom in the world, then wonders, great wonders, shall be wrought on men's souls. By the word and Spirit of Christ, the spiritually blind were enlightened; and those deaf to the calls of God were made to hear them readily. Those unable to do any thing good, by Divine grace were made active therein. Those that knew not how to speak of God or to God, had their lips opened to show forth his praise. When the Holy Ghost came upon the Gentiles that heard the word, then were the fountains of life opened. Most of the earth is still a desert; neither means of grace, spiritual worshippers, nor fruits of holiness, are to be found in it. But the way of religion and godliness shall be laid open. The way of holiness is the way of God's commandment; it is the good old way. And the way to heaven is a plain way. Those knowing but little, and unlearned, shall be kept from missing the road. It shall be a safe way; nothing can do them any real hurt. Christ, the way to God, shall be clearly made known; and the way of a believer's duty shall be plainly marked out. Let us then go forward cheerfully, assured that the end of this way shall be everlasting joy, and rest for the soul. Those who by faith are made citizens of the gospel Zion, rejoice in Christ Jesus; and their sorrows and sighs are made to flee away by Divine consolations. Thus these prophecies conclude. Our joyful hopes and prospects of eternal life should swallow up all the sorrows and all the joys of this present time. But of what avail is it to admire the excellence of God's word, unless we can call its precious promises our own? Do we love God, not only as our Creator, but because he gave his only Son to die for us? And are we walking in the ways of holiness? Let us try ourselves by such plain questions, rather than spend time on things that may be curious and amusing, but are unprofitable.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesHezekiah's sickness and recovery.1–8His thanksgiving.9–22
Hezekiah's illness and restoration (verses 1–8)

When we pray during sickness, God may not give us the same answer that he gave Hezekiah.

But if, through his Spirit, he strengthens our hearts, assures us that our sins are forgiven and teaches us that whether we live or die we belong to him, then our prayers have not been offered in vain.

For the earlier account, see 2 Kings 20:1–11.

Hezekiah thanks the Lord (verses 9–22)

Hezekiah recorded the condition in which he found himself before receiving mercy.

It is good to remember divine kindness, especially kindness received during sickness.

He feared he would no longer see the Lord in the land of the living.

A truly godly person does not seek life merely for its own pleasures, but so that he may serve God and enjoy communion with him.

Our present dwelling resembles a shepherd's temporary hut.

It is poor, cold and insecure; moreover, while we occupy it, we are responsible for work entrusted to us, like a shepherd tending a flock.

Our days resemble a weaver's shuttle (Job 7:6), passing quickly back and forth while each movement leaves a thread behind.

When the woven piece is complete, the Master cuts it from the loom and examines the finished work.

When a faithful person's life ends, burdens and toil end too, and rest begins.

But God determines the length of the cloth—the duration of each life.

During sickness, people often try to calculate how much time remains, but they cannot know.

Their main concern should be reaching the next world in safety.

The more deeply we experience God's kindness, the more we should love him and live for him.

It was through love for perishing sinners that Christ delivered our souls.

Forgiveness does not mean that wrongdoing becomes innocent. It means that sin is not punished as it deserves, because the Lord has provided mercy.

We may remember healing with special gratitude when we see it alongside God's pardon.

Hezekiah regarded every opportunity to glorify God as the business, delight and purpose of life.

After recovering, he resolved to increase his praise and service.

God's promises never remove the obligation to use appropriate means.

Instead, they encourage and strengthen us to employ them.

Life and health are given so that we may glorify God and do good.
classic_reading:
[Isa.38.1-Isa.38.8]
Chapter 38
Hezekiah's sickness and recovery. ( [Isa.38.1-Isa.38.8] Is. 38:1-8) His thanksgiving. ( [Isa.38.9-Isa.38.22] Is. 38:9-22)
Verses 1-8 When we pray in our sickness, though God send not to us such an answer as he here sent to Hezekiah, yet, if by his Spirit he bids us be of good cheer, assures us that our sins are forgiven, and that, whether we live or die, we shall be his, we do not pray in vain. See II Kin. 20:1-11.
[Isa.38.9-Isa.38.22]
Verses 9-22 We have here Hezekiah's thanksgiving. It is well for us to remember the mercies we receive in sickness. Hezekiah records the condition he was in. He dwells upon this; I shall no more see the Lord. A good man wishes not to live for any other end than that he may serve God, and have communion with him. Our present residence is like that of a shepherd in his hut, a poor, mean, and cold lodging, and with a trust committed to our charge, as the shepherd has. Our days are compared to the weaver's shuttle, [Job.7.6] Job 7:6, passing and repassing very swiftly, every throw leaving a thread behind it; and when finished, the piece is cut off, taken out of the loom, and showed to our Master to be judged of. A good man, when his life is cut off, his cares and fatigues are cut off with it, and he rests from his labours. But our times are in God's hand; he has appointed what shall be the length of the piece. When sick, we are very apt to calculate our time, but are still at uncertainty. It should be more our care how we shall get safe to another world. And the more we taste of the loving-kindness of God, the more will our hearts love him, and live to him. It was in love to our poor perishing souls that Christ delivered them. The pardon does not make the sin not to have been sin, but not to be punished as it deserves. It is pleasant to think of our recoveries from sickness, when we see them flowing from the pardon of sin. Hezekiah's opportunity to glorify God in this world, he made the business, and pleasure, and end of life. Being recovered, he resolves to abound in praising and serving God. God's promises are not to do away, but to quicken and encourage the use of means. Life and health are given that we may glorify God and do good.

Comfort: the gospel and the coming of Christ (verses 1–11)

Every human life involves struggle, but the Christian life is especially a warfare.

Yet this struggle will not last forever.

When sin is pardoned, God lovingly removes the deepest cause of our trouble.

Through Christ's death and great atonement, God's mercy is displayed in a way that glorifies his justice.

The satisfaction Christ made through his death has infinite value.

A repentant sinner receives grace more than sufficient for the guilt once carried.

Isaiah's words do refer in part to the Jews' return from Babylon.

But that event is small compared with the fulfillment identified in the New Testament: John the Baptist announcing the arrival of Jesus Christ.

When eastern kings traveled through deserts, people cleared a passage for them and removed obstacles.

So let the Lord prepare our hearts through his word and Spirit.

May proud thoughts be humbled, good desires planted, crooked dispositions straightened, harsh tempers softened and every obstacle to obedience removed.

Everything that belongs to fallen humanity, including its apparent magnificence, withers like grass and flowers.

What good will wealth, status and possessions do for a dying sinner who remains condemned?

God's word accomplishes what human strength cannot.

The good news of Christ's coming is to be announced throughout the world.

Satan is strong and armed, but Jesus Christ is stronger and will accomplish everything he has resolved.

Christ is also the good Shepherd.

He cares tenderly for new converts, weak believers and sorrowful people.

He never demands service or permits suffering without providing grace sufficient to endure it.

May we hear his voice, follow him and prove ourselves to be his sheep.

The Lord's immeasurable power and kindness (verses 12–17)

Compared with the Creator, every creature is small.

When the Lord made the world through his Spirit, nobody advised him or told him how to act.

All the nations are to him like the remaining drop in a bucket beside the ocean, or a tiny amount of dust on a balance compared with the earth.

Yet God's love is astonishing.

Though the world is so small in comparison with him, he gave his only Son to redeem it (John 3:16).

No service rendered by the church can add anything to God's greatness.

Our souls would have been eternally lost had the Father's only Son not given himself for us.

Idols cannot be compared with God (verses 18–26)

Whatever created thing we esteem, love, fear or trust more than God becomes an idol to us, even when we do not make or worship a physical image.

Even people with little to offer may insist on having an idol of their own.

Some spend lavishly to support false gods while begrudging what is devoted to the true God's service.

Isaiah appealed to every generation and nation to recognize the Creator's greatness.

People who refuse this knowledge are often willfully ignorant.

God commands every creature and everything in creation.

The prophet appeals not only to our senses but also to our reasoning.

Consider the stars and the One who created them.

Every member of the heavenly host fulfills his will.

The Lord who governs them is also the One who has spoken his promises and pledged to keep them.

Waiting upon the Lord instead of relying on ourselves (verses 27–31)

God rebuked his people for distrusting him.

They bore the names Jacob and Israel, inherited from a man who discovered that God was faithful through every trial.

Those names reminded them that they were a covenant people.

Many needless fears and complaints disappear when we take time to examine their causes.

It is wrong to entertain unfair thoughts about the Lord; it is worse to turn those thoughts into harmful speech.

The people already knew enough of God's goodness to silence their distrust.

Where God has begun a work of grace, he will complete it.

He helps those who depend humbly upon him and act in the strength he provides.

As each day comes, so does the strength needed for it.

By divine grace believers rise above the world's attractions.

They can run cheerfully in the way of God's commandments.

Guard against unbelief, pride and self-confidence.

If we proceed in our own power, we will faint and fall.

But when our hearts and hopes are set on heaven, God enables us to rise above difficulty and pursue the prize of our calling in Jesus Christ.
classic_reading:
[Isa.40.1-Isa.40.11]
Chapter 40
The preaching of the gospel, and glad tidings of the coming of Christ. ( [Isa.40.1-Isa.40.11] Is. 40:1-11) The almighty power of God. ( [Isa.40.12-Isa.40.17] Is. 40:12-17) The folly of idolatry. ( [Isa.40.18-Isa.40.26] Is. 40:18-26) Against unbelief. ( [Isa.40.27-Isa.40.31] Is. 40:27-31)
Verses 1-11 All human life is a warfare; the Christian life is the most so; but the struggle will not last always. Troubles are removed in love, when sin is pardoned. In the great atonement of the death of Christ, the mercy of God is exercised to the glory of his justice. In Christ, and his sufferings, true penitents receive of the Lord's hand double for all their sins; for the satisfaction Christ made by his death was of infinite value. The prophet had some reference to the return of the Jews from Babylon. But this is a small event, compared with that pointed out by the Holy Ghost in the New Testament, when John the Baptist proclaimed the approach of Christ. When eastern princes marched through desert countries, ways were prepared for them, and hinderances removed. And may the Lord prepare our hearts by the teaching of his word and the convictions of his Spirit, that high and proud thoughts may be brought down, good desires planted, crooked and rugged tempers made straight and softened, and every hinderance removed, that we may be ready for his will on earth, and prepared for his heavenly kingdom. What are all that belongs to fallen man, or all that he does, but as the grass and the flower thereof! And what will all the titles and possessions of a dying sinner avail, when they leave him under condemnation! The word of the Lord can do that for us, which all flesh cannot. The glad tidings of the coming of Christ were to be sent forth to the ends of the earth. Satan is the strong man armed; but our Lord Jesus is stronger; and he shall proceed, and do all that he purposes. Christ is the good Shepherd; he shows tender care for young converts, weak believers, and those of a sorrowful spirit. By his word he requires no more service, and by his providence he inflicts no more trouble, than he will strengthen them for. May we know our Shepherd's voice, and follow him, proving ourselves his sheep.
[Isa.40.12-Isa.40.17]
Verses 12-17 All created beings shrink to nothing in comparison with the Creator. When the Lord, by his Spirit, made the world, none directed his Spirit, or gave advice what to do, or how to do it. The nations, in comparison of him, are as a drop which remains in the bucket, compared with the vast ocean; or as the small dust in the balance, which does not turn it, compared with all the earth. This magnifies God's love to the world, that, though it is of such small account and value with him, yet, for the redemption of it, he gave his only-begotten Son, John 3:16. The services of the church can make no addition to him. Our souls must have perished for ever, if the only Son of the Father had not given himself for us.
[Isa.40.18-Isa.40.26]
Verses 18-26 Whatever we esteem or love, fear or hope in, more than God, that creature we make equal with God, though we do not make images or worship them. He that is so poor, that he has scarcely a sacrifice to offer, yet will not be without a god of his own. They spared no cost upon their idols; we grudge what is spent in the service of our God. To prove the greatness of God, the prophet appeals to all ages and nations. Those who are ignorant of this, are willingly ignorant. God has the command of all creatures, and of all created things. The prophet directs us to use our reason as well as our senses; to consider who created the hosts of heaven, and to pay our homage to Him. Not one fails to fulfil his will. And let us not forget, that He spake all the promises, and engaged to perform them.
[Isa.40.27-Isa.40.31]
Verses 27-31 The people of God are reproved for their unbelief and distrust of God. Let them remember they took the names Jacob and Israel, from one who found God faithful to him in all his straits. And they bore these names as a people in covenant with Him. Many foolish frets, and foolish fears, would vanish before inquiry into the causes. It is bad to have evil thoughts rise in our minds, but worse to turn them into evil words. What they had known, and had heard, was sufficient to silence all these fears and distrusts. Where God had begun the work of grace, he will perfect it. He will help those who, in humble dependence on him, help themselves. As the day, so shall the strength be. In the strength of Divine grace their souls shall ascend above the world. They shall run the way of God's commandments cheerfully. Let us watch against unbelief, pride, and self-confidence. If we go forth in our own strength, we shall faint, and utterly fall; but having our hearts and our hopes in heaven, we shall be carried above all difficulties, and be enabled to lay hold of the prize of our high calling in Christ Jesus.
